clue.text: Iced drinks at last!

definitions.meaning: a cobbler is a long iced drink of wine or sherry, sugar and fruit
shoe-menders do their work at a last, the foot-shaped block

explanation.surface: A thirsty person finally greets the arrival of cold drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as relief that drinks have come at last; really 'at last' describes shoe-menders, who work at a last.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a chilled cocktail of wine and fruit and the tradesmen who mend shoes on a last.

clue.text: Small output of composer in a swimsuit?

definitions.meaning: a composer who wrote just one work has a tiny output
a swimming costume made as a single garment

explanation.surface: A composer, dressed for the beach, produces very little music.
explanation.definitionFit: A single work is a composer's smallest possible output, and a costume in one garment is a type of swimwear.

clue.text: Quantum leap-stroke of luck finished in America

parts.note: a lucky break is a stroke of luck
Americans say they are through when they are finished

explanation.surface: A great advance turns out to be a lucky chance that has run its course in the States.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramatic advance in knowledge or progress is a sudden great leap forward.

clue.text: Bring out early opening with lawful following

indicators.note: the opening of the word early is its first letter

parts.note: licit means allowed by law

explanation.surface: Someone draws out an early start, with legality coming afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw out a response or information is to extract it from someone.

clue.text: Most of scandal is bogus

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter

parts.note: a shame is a scandalous disgrace

explanation.surface: A claim that the bulk of a scandal is fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fake or pretended is a counterfeit, not genuine.

clue.text: News-round received?

parts.note: a round of ammunition is a bullet
something received has come in

explanation.surface: A news round-up is taken in by listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: A short broadcast or printed report gives the latest news.

clue.text: Eastern nurse needs a morning visiting a hospital

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for the morning hours
H is the abbreviation for hospital on maps and signs

explanation.surface: A nurse in the East must make a morning call at a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: In India and the Far East this is the word for a nursemaid or children's maid.

clue.text: Not made ready for publication, tune died out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A song fades away before anyone has prepared it for print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the letters of TUNE DIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Text that has not been revised or corrected is still raw, as yet unprepared for print.

clue.text: Poet introduces English doctor in hospital

indicators.note: the poet's name takes in another letter, as if introducing it into himself

parts.note: A. E. Housman was the English poet of A Shropshire Lad

explanation.surface: A poet presents an English doctor who works at a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: A. E. HOUSMAN wrote A Shropshire Lad; 'introduces' puts E inside his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A junior resident doctor in a British hospital was traditionally called by this title.

clue.text: Note, summer in France could be fair

parts.note: F is a musical note
été is French for summer

explanation.surface: A French summer could bring an outdoor fair, someone notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A village gala with stalls and games is a type of fair.

clue.text: Finished and polished

definitions.meaning: achieved or completed, as a task done

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both completed, as a task achieved, and highly skilled, as a refined performer.

clue.text: The case for arms limitation?

parts.note: reads like a disarmament argument, but describes a garment that encases a person and restrains their arms

explanation.definitionFit: A restraining jacket with long sleeves tied behind confines a person's arms.

clue.text: Dry sort who would not get 1 across?

definitions.text: Dry sort who would not get 1 across?

parts.words: Dry sort who would not get 1 across?
parts.note: a dry person here is one who abstains from alcohol, so would refuse the iced alcoholic drinks of the other clue

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains from all alcohol is dry, so would not order an alcoholic iced drink.

clue.text: Door-fastening should be long at church opening

explanation.surface: A door catch ought to be long, at the church entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple bar that drops into a catch is used to secure a door or gate.

clue.text: See sailor achieve his object

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
to get something is to achieve or obtain it

explanation.surface: Watch the seaman reach his goal.
explanation.definitionFit: An aim or goal that one tries to hit is one's object.

clue.text: One listener to president in conference, say…

parts.note: an ear is the organ one listens with

explanation.surface: Someone listens to a president speaking at a conference.
explanation.walkthrough: Conference is a variety of pear, so 'conference, say' is a definition by example, not a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Conference is a well-known British variety of this fruit, so it is an example.

clue.text: Through-lines can be troublesome, wayward

parts.note: per means through or by means of
verse is lines of poetry

explanation.surface: Lines running through can cause difficulty and go astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone contrary and unreasonable is stubbornly wayward.

clue.text: … cause to attack minutes when sent back

indicators.note: sent back means the word for minutes is written backwards

parts.note: minutes of a meeting are notes

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to attack the minutes of a meeting when they are returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns NOTES round to give SETON.
explanation.definitionFit: To set dogs on someone is to make them attack.

clue.text: Bad day for Caesar in parade (but not the main event)

indicators.note: in places the day for Caesar inside the word for parade

parts.note: to parade something is to show it off
Caesar was killed on the Ides of March

explanation.surface: Caesar's unlucky day comes at a parade, a minor attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March, the IDES that goes inside SHOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor attraction beside the principal one at a fair or circus is secondary.

clue.text: I make an offer in the same place, in reference-books

definitions.text: in the same place, in reference-books

parts.note: to bid is to make an offer at auction

explanation.surface: Someone offers to buy something at the same spot mentioned in a reference work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin abbreviation ibidem, used in footnotes, means from the same source already cited.

clue.text: Main road runs up to port in Alabama, still

indicators.note: in a down clue, running up means the road's name is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI
Mobile is a port city in Alabama

explanation.surface: A trunk road heads up towards an Alabama port, and is still there.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the main London–Leeds motorway; 'runs up' turns MI into IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmoving and motionless, anything still stays put.

clue.text: Reimbursement gives pleasure when overdrawn

indicators.note: pleasure is set within, held while the account is overdrawn, so it sits inside

parts.note: an overdrawn account is in the red
fun is enjoyment or pleasure

explanation.surface: Getting money back is a delight for someone overdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: An overdrawn account is 'in the red', so FUN goes inside RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A repayment of money already spent is a reimbursement.

clue.text: Punishment for going over the bar?

definitions.meaning: the athletics event where competitors leap over a raised bar

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the athletics leaping event and, in British idiom 'for the', impending trouble or a telling-off.

clue.text: Means of avoiding something, say? Leave at once!

definitions.meaning: an escape clause or excuse that lets one avoid a duty
a rude order to go away immediately

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an escape route from an obligation and a curt order to depart.

clue.text: So keen, haunts cities when travelling

indicators.note: travelling suggests the letters are on the move into a new order

explanation.surface: A keen tourist frequents city after city on a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Eager and full of zeal, a keen person is wholeheartedly eager.

clue.text: Sound horn in both directions

indicators.note: the word reads the same forwards and backwards, the same in both directions

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A driver honks in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: To blast a car horn briefly is to give a short honk.

clue.text: Queen occupying most of extension

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter

parts.note: an annex is an extension to a building

explanation.surface: A queen lives in most of the new wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne was a British monarch, so she is an example of a queen.

clue.text: Can sovereign retire to make scarves?

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the words for can and sovereign are read backwards together

parts.note: a tin is a can
K is the abbreviation for king, a sovereign

explanation.surface: Can a monarch withdraw into private life to make woollens?
explanation.walkthrough: 'retire' turns TIN plus K (king) backwards as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarves are made by looping wool on needles.

clue.text: Easy means of getting into Oxford, perhaps?

definitions.text: Easy means of getting into Oxford, perhaps?

parts.words: Easy means of getting into Oxford, perhaps?
parts.note: suggests a back door into the university, but an Oxford is a style of laced shoe and this tool eases the foot in

explanation.definitionFit: A curved tool helps a foot slide into a tight shoe such as an Oxford brogue.

clue.text: Qualified English openers, not common people

annotationWithheld.why: Qualified English openers, not common people (8): E + TITLED (not common people) leaves N to come from 'openers' of 'not', so 'not' would do two jobs; no sound parse found
annotationWithheld.clue: Qualified English openers, not common people
